title: From random walks to Brownian motion
objectives: Shrink a random walk’s steps to get Brownian motion.

screens.prose: Topic 3.2 is optional: it serves derivatives pricing and desk quant roles, so traders and researchers may skip it. A fair coin walk takes 16 steps in one unit of time. Each step is $\pm\tfrac14$.

params.xLabel: Step (16 steps make one unit of time)

screens.question: What is the variance of where the walk ends?

hints.text: One step is $\pm\tfrac14$. What is its variance?
One step has variance $(\tfrac14)^2 = \tfrac1{16}$.
Independent steps add their variances: $16 \times \tfrac1{16}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the variance of one step, then add it up over 16 steps.

byKey.unit: 16 is the variance for steps of $\pm 1$. These steps are $\pm\tfrac14$, so each adds only $\tfrac1{16}$.
byKey.sizes: You added the 16 step sizes. Variances add, and one step's variance is $(\tfrac14)^2$.
byKey.one: $\tfrac1{16}$ is the variance of one step. The walk takes 16 of them.

explain.text: Each step has variance $\tfrac1{16}$, and 16 independent steps add to 1. The step size $\tfrac14 = 1/\sqrt{16}$ was chosen to make that happen. Next we see what this choice does as the steps get finer.

screens.prose: Now take $n$ steps of size $1/\sqrt{n}$ in the same unit of time. Slide $n$ from 4 to 1,024, and draw new paths. The dashed curves are $\pm\sqrt{t}$, where $t$ is the share of the time used.

params.xLabel: Step (all the steps fill one unit of time)

screens.question: As $n$ grows, what happens to the spread of the paths at the end?

options.text: It stays about the same: most paths end within 2 of 0

options.why: You remembered the unscaled walk of markov l9. Here each step shrinks to $1/\sqrt{n}$, which cancels that growth.

options.text: It shrinks towards 0 as the steps get tiny
options.why: You saw the steps shrink and expected the motion to vanish. There are more of them, and their variances still add to 1.

options.text: It stays the same, and the paths become smooth curves
options.why: The spread holds, but look closely at $n = 1{,}024$: the paths get rougher, not smoother.

hints.text: Compare the outer paths at $n = 4$ and at $n = 1{,}024$.
The dashed curves end at $\pm 1$ for every $n$.

feedback.correct: The spread holds still while the paths get rougher.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the ends of the paths against the dashed curves as you slide $n$.

explain.text: Each of the $n$ steps has variance $1/n$, so the endpoint always has variance 1. The paths get rougher, but their spread holds still. Their limit is a random continuous curve, which we name next.

screens.prose: The limit of these walks is **Brownian motion**, written $W_t$. The scaling is the whole trick. From markov l9, a fair walk of $n$ steps of $\pm 1$ has $\operatorname{Var}(S_n) = n$.

params.xLabel: Step (all the steps fill one unit of time)

screens.question: With $n = 400$ steps of $\pm 1$, what number $c$ makes $\operatorname{Var}(cS_{400}) = 1$?

hints.text: Scaling by $c$ multiplies a variance by $c^2$.
You need $c^2 \times 400 = 1$.

feedback.correct: $c = 1/\sqrt{400} = 0.05$, the step size on the canvas.

byKey.over-n: You scaled by $1/n$. That gives variance $400/400^2 = 1/400$, far below 1.
byKey.root: 20 is $\sqrt{400}$, the sd of $S_{400}$. Divide by it: $c = 1/20$.
byKey.var: 400 is the variance of $S_{400}$. The scale is one over its square root.

explain.text: $\operatorname{Var}(cS_n) = c^2 n$, so $c = 1/\sqrt{n} = 0.05$. Any other power of $n$ sends the variance to 0 or to infinity. Only $1/\sqrt{n}$ leaves a motion that neither dies nor explodes.

screens.prose: The same walks, a quarter of the way through: after 100 of the 400 steps, which is time $t = 0.25$.

params.xLabel: Step (all the steps fill one unit of time)

screens.question: What is the standard deviation of $W_{0.25}$?

widget.label: Standard deviation of W at t = 0.25

hints.text: How many steps has the walk taken by $t = 0.25$, and what does each add to the variance?
100 steps, each with variance $\tfrac1{400}$.
The variance is $\tfrac{100}{400} = 0.25$. Take the square root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the steps up to the line, add their variances, then take the square root.

byKey.var: 0.25 is the variance of $W_{0.25}$. The sd is its square root.
byKey.sq: You squared 0.25. The variance is $t$ itself, and the sd is $\sqrt{t}$.
byKey.whole: 1 is the sd at the end, $t = 1$. Only a quarter of the steps have happened.

explain.text: By time $t$ the walk has taken $nt$ steps of variance $1/n$, so $\operatorname{Var}(W_t) = t$. Here $\operatorname{Var}(W_{0.25}) = 0.25$ and the sd is 0.5. The dashed curve sits at $\pm 0.5$ where it crosses the line.

screens.prose: Each bar counts endpoints $W_1$ of walks with 64 steps of $\pm\tfrac18$. Run the simulation. The curve is the standard normal density, scaled to the bins. By the central limit theorem, $W_1 \sim N(0, 1)$.
screens.question: Use the normal: what is $P(W_1 > 1)$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: $W_1$ is standard normal, so $P(W_1 > 1) = 1 - \Phi(1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\Phi(1)$, the chance of being below 1, and take it from 1.

byKey.two: 0.3173 is the chance of ending more than 1 away on either side. The question asks only above 1.
byKey.cdf: 0.8413 is $\Phi(1)$, the chance of ending below 1.
byKey.half: 0.5 is the chance of ending above 0. The level here is 1.

explain.text: $P(W_1 > 1) = 1 - \Phi(1) = 0.1587$. The bars hug the normal curve after 10,000 walks. So the normal answers questions about $W_1$ even though each walk was built from coins.

screens.prose: A colleague scales each step by $1/n$ instead, to average the coin flips. Here are 20 of their walks with $n = 400$ steps of $\pm\tfrac{1}{400}$, on the same axes as before.

params.xLabel: Step (all the steps fill one unit of time)

screens.question: What does their walk become as $n$ grows?

options.text: A flat line at 0: the endpoint has sd $1/\sqrt{n}$

options.why: You treated $1/n$ as a rescaled $1/\sqrt{n}$. The variance $n \times 1/n^2 = 1/n$ goes to 0, so nothing is left.

options.text: A straight line whose slope the coin sets
options.why: A fair coin has no drift. Averaging leaves its mean, which is 0.
Blowing up needs steps bigger than $1/\sqrt{n}$. Steps of $1/n$ are smaller.

hints.text: What is the variance of the endpoint with steps of $1/n$?
Each step has variance $1/n^2$, and there are $n$ of them.
The endpoint has variance $1/n$, which goes to 0.

feedback.correct: Averaging kills the motion: the endpoint tends to 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the endpoint's variance with steps of $1/n$.

byKey.bm: You expected averaging to keep the motion. Averaging is the law of large numbers: the walk settles on its mean, 0.
byKey.line: You looked for a trend in the average. The coin is fair, so the average heads for 0.
byKey.explode: You read smaller steps as wilder paths. Steps of $1/n$ make the paths flatter.

explain.text: With steps of $1/n$ the endpoint is the average of $n$ coins, with variance $1/n$. The law of large numbers sends it to 0. Only $1/\sqrt{n}$ keeps a variance of 1.

screens.prose: Bias the coin a little: $p = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\mu\sqrt{\Delta t}$, with $\Delta t = 1/n$. Here $n = 400$, so $\sqrt{\Delta t} = 0.05$. Slide the drift $\mu$ and watch the dashed mean path.

params.xLabel: Step (all the steps fill one unit of time)

screens.question: With $\mu = 1$, where does the mean path end at $t = 1$?

hints.text: One step has mean $(2p - 1) \times 0.05$.
400 steps, each of mean $0.05 \times 0.05 = 0.0025$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the mean of one step, $(2p - 1) \times 0.05$, then add 400 of them.

byKey.unscaled: 20 is $400 \times (2p - 1)$ for steps of $\pm 1$. These steps are only 0.05 tall.
byKey.fair: A bias of 0.025 looks tiny, but 400 steps add it up.
byKey.one: 0.0025 is the mean of one step. The walk takes 400.

explain.text: Each step has mean $\mu\sqrt{\Delta t} \times \sqrt{\Delta t} = \mu\Delta t$, so the $n$ steps add up to $\mu$. The spread is still about 1, as $p$ barely moves from $\tfrac12$. The limit is $\mu t + W_t$: Brownian motion with drift.

screens.prose: You have built **Brownian motion**: $n$ steps of $\pm 1/\sqrt{n}$ per unit of time, with $n \to \infty$. At every time $t$, $$W_t \sim N(0, t), \qquad \operatorname{sd}(W_t) = \sqrt{t}.$$ The spread grows like $\sqrt{t}$, not like $t$.
screens.question: Which distribution does $W_4$ have?

options.why: You used 2 as the variance. 2 is the sd, $\sqrt{4}$.
You squared the time. The variance is $t$ itself.
You gave it a mean. Without drift the mean stays 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The variance of $W_t$ is $t$, and the mean is 0.

explain.text: $W_4 \sim N(0, 4)$, so its sd is 2. Four units of time give twice the spread of one. Shreve (Stochastic Calculus for Finance II, section 3.2) builds it from scaled walks in just this way.

screens.title: The scaled walk in code
screens.prose: Build the walk in NumPy. `scaled_walk(n, seed)` turns the 0-or-1 draws into steps of $\pm 1$, scales them by $1/\sqrt{n}$ and returns the $n + 1$ values from 0. `var_at_one(n, paths, seed)` returns the sample variance of $W_1$ over the rows of `flips`.
screens.question: Complete `scaled_walk` and `var_at_one`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def scaled_walk(n, seed):
    """n steps of +-1/sqrt(n) from 0: n + 1 values."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    steps = rng.integers(0, 2, n) * 2 - 1
    ...

def var_at_one(n, paths, seed):
    """Sample variance (ddof=1) of W_1 over walks."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    flips = rng.integers(0, 2, (paths, n)) * 2 - 1
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: the walk's values to 6 places on seeds 0 and 3, its length and start, its end on seed 5, var_at_one to 6 places on seed 1, and var_at_one within 0.0425 (three standard errors) of 1 on seeds 2 and 3.

hints.text: `np.cumsum` adds the steps up; put a 0 in front with `np.concatenate`.
Divide the running sum by `np.sqrt(n)`.
For `var_at_one`, sum each row (`axis=1`), divide by `np.sqrt(n)`, then `np.var(..., ddof=1)`.

feedback.correct: The walk and its endpoint variance both check out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your walk on seed 0 with the example, value by value.

explain.text: The running sum of $\pm 1$ steps, divided by $\sqrt{n}$, is the scaled walk. On seed 1 the sample variance of $W_1$ over 10,000 walks is 1.0054, within one standard error (0.014) of 1. A sum over each row gives all the endpoints in one line.

screens.prose: A desk's 1-day 99% value at risk (VaR) is £2.0m. Its daily P&L moves are taken as independent with equal variance, like Brownian increments. The regulator asks for a 10-day VaR.
screens.question: What is the 10-day VaR, in £ million? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Variance grows like time, so the sd grows like the square root of time.
Ten days have $\sqrt{10} = 3.162$ times the 1-day sd.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale the 1-day VaR by the square root of the number of days.

byKey.linear: You scaled by 10 days. Independent days add variances, so the sd grows by $\sqrt{10}$ only.
byKey.same: The risk does grow with the horizon, like $\sqrt{t}$.
byKey.var: You scaled the squared VaR, $2^2 \times 10$. Take the square root: $\sqrt{40} = 6.32$.

explain.text: Independent days add variances, so the 10-day sd is $\sqrt{10}$ times the 1-day sd: £2.0m $\times 3.162$ = £6.32m. The rule fails when days are correlated: P&L momentum makes the true figure larger. Fat tails break it too, as the 99% point is then no fixed number of sds.

ideas: A fair walk with $n$ steps of $\pm 1/\sqrt{n}$ per unit of time has variance $t$ at time $t$, for every $n$.
As $n \to \infty$ the walk becomes Brownian motion $W_t$, and by the central limit theorem $W_t \sim N(0, t)$.
Spread grows like $\sqrt{t}$: a 10-day risk is $\sqrt{10}$ times a 1-day risk when days are independent.

formula.name: Brownian motion as a scaled walk
formula.note: Scale by $1/\sqrt{n}$: $1/n$ flattens the walk, anything bigger blows it up.

summary.trap: Scaling by $1/n$ averages the steps away and leaves a flat line at 0.

quiz.prose: A fair walk takes 900 steps of $\pm\tfrac1{30}$ in one unit of time.
quiz.question: What is the standard deviation of where it ends?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the 900 step variances, then take the square root.

byKey.sizes: You added the step sizes, $900 \times \tfrac1{30}$. Variances add, not sizes.
byKey.one: $\tfrac1{30}$ is one step. The walk takes 900.
byKey.var: 900 is the variance with steps of $\pm 1$. These steps are $\tfrac1{30}$ tall.

explain.text: Each step has variance $\tfrac1{900}$, and 900 of them add to 1. Steps of $1/\sqrt{n}$ always give an sd of 1 at time 1. That is why they build Brownian motion.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Standardise with the sd of $W_4$, which is $\sqrt{4}$.

byKey.sd1: You used sd 1. $W_4$ has variance 4 and sd 2.
byKey.sd4: You divided by 4, the variance. Divide by the sd, 2.

explain.text: $W_4 \sim N(0, 4)$ has sd 2, so $P(W_4 > 2) = P(Z > 1) = 1 - \Phi(1) = 0.1587$. A level of $\sqrt{t}$ at time $t$ is always one sd away. So this chance is the same at every $t$.

quiz.prose: Scale a fair $\pm 1$ walk of $n$ steps by $n^{-0.4}$ instead of $n^{-0.5}$.
quiz.question: As $n \to \infty$, what happens to the variance of the endpoint?

options.why: Only $n^{-0.5}$ gives variance 1. Here the variance is $n \times n^{-0.8} = n^{0.2}$.
That happens for powers below $-0.5$, such as $1/n$. $n^{-0.4}$ shrinks the steps less.

explain.text: The endpoint's variance is $n \times (n^{-0.4})^2 = n^{0.2}$, which grows without bound. A power below $-0.5$ sends it to 0 instead. Only $-0.5$ gives a limit that stays random and finite.

quiz.prose: A risk manager scales a 1-day VaR by $\sqrt{10}$ to get a 10-day VaR.
quiz.question: When does that understate the 10-day risk?

options.text: When good and bad days cluster, so returns are positively autocorrelated

options.why: Negative autocorrelation makes days cancel. The true 10-day risk is then smaller than the rule says.

options.text: When the mean daily P&L is zero
options.why: A zero mean is what the rule assumes. It does not break it.
The rule scales any level of volatility. What matters is independence, not the level.

feedback.correct: Positive autocorrelation adds covariance terms, so the 10-day variance exceeds 10 days' worth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which assumption behind adding variances could fail.

explain.text: Adding variances needs independent days. Positive autocorrelation adds positive covariance terms, so the 10-day variance exceeds ten times the 1-day variance. Then $\sqrt{10}$ understates the risk.
